extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, creators, and scholars interested in parody and humor
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative distinctions for producing or analysing parodies across media (literature, music, film, internet culture), including genre distinctions, forms, legal considerations, and ethical/tactical advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A parody is a creative work designed to imitate, comment on, and/or mock its subject by means of satirical or ironic imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often targets an original work or an aspect of it (theme/content, author, style), but can also target a real-life person, event, or movement. Parody may be imitation that is playful and not always at the expense of the parodied text (cf. Linda Hutcheon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Target specificity (specific vs general parody / spoof)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parody is derivative of a specific work ('specific parody') or a general genre ('general parody' or 'spoof').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A spoof typically mocks an entire genre by exaggerating conventions and clichés for humorous effect, whereas a parody imitates and mocks a specific, recognizable work or the characteristic style of a particular author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent: playful humor vs satiric critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Parodies are more focused on producing playful humor and do not always attack or criticize their target; satire is meant to make fun of the real world and provoke correction or punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A work may contain both parody and satire; it remains parody as long as the 'light verse with modest aspirations' dominates. Satirical intent (attacking a vice, social ill) differentiates true satire from playful parody.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformative/commentary function for legal fair use (United States)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parodies are protected under US fair use doctrine more successfully when the usage is transformative, e.g., providing critique or commentary on the original work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Campbell v. Acuff‑Rose (2 Live Crew) upheld parody as fair use because it was a distinctive, transformative work designed to ridicule the original; contrast Dr. Seuss Enterprises v. Penguin Books where the Ninth Circuit denied fair use because the work lacked a sufficient commentary function on the original.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional copyright exceptions and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal protection for parody varies by country: US relies on fair use/transformative analysis; Canada historically lacked explicit parody/satire protection (changed with 2012 legislation); UK Section 30A (Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988) provides an exception for parody, caricature or pastiche.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creators must consider local law: some countries criminalize or punish parody (e.g., UAE, North Korea). UK law does not define 'parody' but IPO guidance suggests imitation for humorous or satirical effect; Canada’s Copyright Modernization Act 2012 recognized parody/satire as fair dealing purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal parody (economy and rigor)
rubrics_metrics.description: The most rigorous and elegant form of parody is a minimal parody that literally reprises a known text and gives it a new meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gérard Genette praises economical parodies that reuse a text with minimal change to produce new interpretation; 'blank parody' (skeleton form in new context without ridicule) is a related technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: pastiche
rubrics_metrics.description: Pastiche imitates a work like a parody does, but unlike parody a pastiche is neither transformative of the original nor humorous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fredric Jameson and others call pastiche a 'blank parody' — imitation without the satirical/humorous intent. Use pastiche when the aim is homage or stylistic continuity rather than mockery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: travesty
rubrics_metrics.description: A travesty imitates and transforms a work but focuses more on satirization; the harmless playfulness of parody is lost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Travesty is more aggressively critical than parody and targets the original in a way intended to attack or degrade rather than playfully imitate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: skit
rubrics_metrics.description: Skits imitate works 'in a satirical regime' but, unlike travesty, do not transform the source material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skits commonly reproduce recognizable material within a satirical performance context; they rely on audience recognition but may not reconfigure the source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: burlesque
rubrics_metrics.description: Burlesque primarily targets heroic poems and theater to degrade popular heroes and gods, mocking common genre tropes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burlesque can be described as 'parodic anti-heroic drama' and historically aimed to lower the elevated subject to comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical parody conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: In classical music 'parody' can mean reworking one kind of composition into another; in contemporary usage musical parody usually has humorous or satirical intent, lifting familiar musical ideas or lyrics into incongruous contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples include parody masses that quote motets; modern examples include Weird Al Yankovic, who often parodies particular popular songs. Musical parody may imitate a composer’s style or a genre; quotation of recognizable material is common and often essential for audience recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kenneth Baker's five forms of poetic parody
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic parody can take five main forms: (1) attack the author parodied; (2) pastiche the author's style; (3) reverse/undercut the sentiments of the poem; (4) use the target poem as matrix to insert unrelated humorous material; (5) topical parody using a well-known verse format to target contemporary issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: mimicry of Wordsworth (attack), Henry Reed's pastiche of T. S. Eliot (style pastiche), Monty Python's lampooning (reversal), inserting unrelated material into Hamlet lines (matrix), topical parodies addressing public figures/events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-parody
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-parody is a subset in which artists parody their own work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used deliberately by creators (e.g., Ricky Gervais's Extras) to playfully critique or rework their style/brand; can function as self-aware commentary or brand extension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody as genre-life-cycle device
rubrics_metrics.description: Some genre theorists see parody as a natural development in the life cycle of a genre: when a genre's formula grows tired, it retains value only as parody.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parody in this view inverts audience expectations established by earlier exemplars (e.g., Westerns passing into parody stage). Parodic inversion can renew, critique, or register change within a genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recontextualizing/blank parody (postmodern use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern/postmodern parody often reuses elements of older works in new contexts without necessarily ridiculing them, serving to connect with the past or to target something else.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Joyce's Ulysses or T. S. Eliot's The Waste Land; such parodies may be less about mockery and more about reconfiguration and intertextual dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social and political functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Parody is often used to make social or political statements, e.g., Swift's 'A Modest Proposal' or television programs that parody news/talk formats to satirize political and social trends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parody can shape public perception of political figures (e.g., SNL sketches). Creators must consider the intended political effect and whether parody serves critique, commentary, protest, or merely entertainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity, ethics, and editorial judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: When addressing traumatic or sensitive events, creators and editors must judge whether parody is appropriate — questions of timing, audience readiness, and what is 'funny' are central.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The Onion's internal debate about publishing post‑9/11 material; editors should weigh potential divisions in staff/audience and ethical implications before publishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-generated parody / parody generators
rubrics_metrics.description: Parody generators produce syntactically correct but usually meaningless text in the style of a technical paper or particular writer, often to satirize or demonstrate similarity between generated and 'real' examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques include Markov chains or hand-coded templates; generated texts can range from tweets to essays and are used for travesty/satirical purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition requirement (audience familiarity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective parody depends on audience recognition of what is being imitated — the parody's humor often relies on invoking the 'heart' of the original (a recognisable line, riff, or style).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal and creative analyses note that copying a distinctive element may be necessary for comedic effect (as in Campbell v. Acuff‑Rose), but creators should balance recognisability with transformation to avoid infringement.
